en: Translated by Imperial Decree by Song Guṇabhadra; annotated together by Imperial Decree by the Subject Monk Zongle,
Abbot of the Chan Temple Shanshi in the Celestial Realm of the Great Ming,
and the Subject Monk Ruxi, Abbot of the Lecture Hall Temple Yanfu.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to know the manifestation of his own mind—the realm of false discrimination consisting of the grasped and the grasper—he should leave behind crowds, worldly customs, and sleep; throughout the first, middle, and last watches of the night, he should constantly awaken himself and practice skillful means. He should distance himself from the discourses and doctrines of evil views, as well as the characteristics of the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and he should penetrate the nature of false discrimination as the manifestation of his own mind."

The preceding clarification of reality is certainly not within the realm of non-Buddhists or those of the Lesser Vehicle; nevertheless, if one can cultivate the Dharma-gates inherently possessed by the mind, why worry that success will not be achieved?
Therefore, I here offer this exhortation:
all objects of perception within the realm of direct experience do not arise apart from one's own mind; yet, through delusion and lack of awakening, one grasps at them with false conceptualization.
To speak of "appropriating" refers to the subject that grasps.
As for "and that which is grasped," it refers to the object of apprehension.

To understand the false and manifest the true, one should dwell alone, far removed from the mundane, and free from all dullness and distraction; one should maintain vigilance during the first, middle, and last watches of the night—this is what is called the skillful method of practice.

However, evil views as found in the scriptures and treatises are the root of external paths, and the mark of emptiness in the Lesser Vehicle is the affliction of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. If one understands how to distance oneself from these, one will be able to penetrate the marks of delusive thoughts manifested by one's own mind and thereby realize the realm of ultimate reality.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
Having established themselves in the characteristics of wisdom, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently cultivate and study the three aspects of supreme noble gnosis."
What are the three characteristics of noble wisdom that one should diligently cultivate?
They are: the characteristic of non-existence, the characteristic of the sphere of the self-vow of all Buddhas, and the characteristic of the ultimate realization of noble self-aware wisdom.

Having attained this through practice, one is able to relinquish the mental characteristics of the lame donkey and wisdom, and attains the eighth stage of the Supreme Son; thereupon, one cultivates and gives rise to the three marks above that.
Mahāmati! The characteristic of non-existence refers to the characteristics of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and outsiders; it arises from their cultivation. Mahāmati!
Regarding the characteristic of the station of one’s own vows: it refers to that which arises from the cultivation of the stations of the vows made by previous Buddhas. Mahāmati!

Regarding the characteristic of the ultimate realization of noble self-awareness-wisdom: it is the non-attachment to the characteristics of all phenomena, the attainment of the body of the illusion-like samādhi, and the arising of the conduct that advances toward the stages of the Buddhas.
Mahāmati! These are called the three characteristics of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
One who accomplishes these three characteristics of noble wisdom can reach the ultimate realm of self-realized noble wisdom; therefore, Mahāmati!
"One should diligently cultivate and study the three marks of noble wisdom.

The aforementioned state of the Dharmakāya is the ultimate ground of the Tathāgata; for a practitioner who wishes to reach this ground, there is no way to advance without wisdom. Therefore, the marks of wisdom are established as the basis upon which those who train rely and abide.
If one does not advance in one's efforts, by what means can accomplishment be achieved?
Therefore, the admonition and exhortation states:
"One should diligently practice and study the three aspects of the supreme noble wisdom."
Furthermore, fearing that Mahāmati had not yet mastered the three characteristics, [the Buddha] again questioned and explained them.
However, these three characteristics are beyond the reach of the followers of the Two Vehicles; therefore, they are likened to a lame donkey.
The "Sons of the Most Victorious One" refers to Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage.
Because they do not share [the same realization] with those of the Two Vehicles, it is said that they "are able to relinquish.
This is because although this sutra belongs to the Mahāyāna, it also incorporates the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
"Arising through cultivation" refers to the arising of noble wisdom through practice.
"The mark of non-existence" means the absence of the marks of the two vehicles and external paths.
"The mark of the sphere of one's own vows" refers to the fact that all Buddhas establish vows and engage in cultivation from the very beginning.
The characteristic of the ultimate realization of noble wisdom is the characteristic of the wisdom of the middle way realized within oneself.
Since the middle way is free from the characteristics of the two extremes of existence and non-existence, it is said that there is nothing to which one clings or adheres.
The *samādhi-body* is precisely the *saṃbhogakāya*.

Regarding the phrase "in all places of the stages" and so forth: it means that the *nirmāṇakāya* pervades all Buddha-fields, manifesting the progression toward and attainment of the fruit; therefore, it is called "arising through practice."
The exhortation to practice together may be understood as before.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly of great Bodhisattvas, [recited] the *Sūtra on the Differentiation of the Self-Nature of Noble Wisdom-Activity* (Āryajñānavastuvibhāgasvabhāva-sūtra), and, sustained by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I only pray that you will explain for me the *Āryajñānavastupravibhaktasvabhāva-sūtra* consisting of one hundred and eight phrases, which distinguishes the basis [of phenomena].
The five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness are all the matters of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) taught in this sūtra.

The bodhisattvas, having already heard the exposition on the eight consciousnesses, now desire to hear the teaching on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*); therefore, Mahāmati makes this request once again.
The term "Sūtra on the Natures" is used here to refer to the general category while encompassing its specific instances.

Regarding the statement "the basis for the differentiation of the one hundred and eight phrases," this means that the one hundred and eight phrases take the differentiated self-nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as their basis.

"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, relying upon this differentiation, teaches that the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva enters into the imagined nature of both specific and common characteristics. Because he explains the imagined nature through differentiation, he is able to skillfully know and universally observe the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*), purify and eliminate false imaginings, illuminate the various stages (*bhūmi*), and transcend all the pleasures of meditative concentration belonging to Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists. He observes the inconceivable sphere of activity of the Tathāgata and becomes definitively detached from the five dharmas and the [three] natures."

The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, having well-adorned themselves with the wisdom of the Dharma-body, manifest illusory realms and ascend to all Buddha-fields, the Tuṣita palaces, and even up to the Akaniṣṭha palaces, thereby attaining the eternally abiding Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata, out of compassion for those bodhisattvas who cling to the specific and general characteristics of phenomena as being real, teaches the gateway to the meaning of the imagined nature and its distinctions.
Once they understand this meaning and investigate it thoroughly, they will become free from the clinging to the two selves of persons and phenomena.

Once grasping has been relinquished, one enters the various stages (*bhūmi*), thereby transcending the meditative concentrations of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, and entering with ease into the inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata.
Thus, the false attachments to the five dharmas and the three natures are relinquished without being separated from them.
The adornment of the wisdom of the Dharma-body is the perfection of the fruit of one's own practice.
The manifestation of illusory realms is the appearance of lands to transform others.

As for all Buddha-fields and celestial palaces, wherever there are sentient beings capable of being transformed, [the Buddha] manifests birth therein and attains equal and perfect enlightenment without exception.
Tuṣita is translated here as "Contentment," meaning that one knows the limit and sufficiency regarding the five desires.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"There is a class of non-Buddhists who engage in false conceptualization and attachment to 'nothingness. They perceive that causes have been exhausted and thus conceive the notion that a rabbit has no horns."
"Just as a rabbit has no horns, so it is with all dharmas.

Mahāmati, furthermore, there are other non-Buddhists who perceive seeds, qualities (*guṇa*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), substances (*dravya*), and spatial dimensions as distinct entities. Having perceived them, they become attached to the notion that while a rabbit has no horns, a cow—which is a spatially extended entity—does possess horns."
The views of the non-Buddhists do not exceed two types:

first, the calculation of non-existence, which holds that all phenomena perish according to their causes and that no further cause exists; like a rabbit has no horns, so too are all phenomena—this is the view of annihilationism.
Second is the calculation of existence, which views that the great elements (*mahābhūta*) arise based upon atoms (*paramāṇu*).
"Great elements" refers to the four great elements.
*Guṇa* (求那) is translated as "based upon" (*āśrita*).
*Dravya* (dhāra-bhāva) is translated as "dust" (*reṇu*).
To falsely calculate distinctions regarding the dimensions and locations of objects such as dust, and to form the notion that "an ox has horns," is the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).

“Mahāmati! Those who fall into these two views do not understand that [all things] are merely the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*). Their own mental objects increase through false discrimination (*vikalpa*), and they establish the measure of the root of false discrimination based on their perceptions of the body and its enjoyments.”
Mahāmati! The nature of all phenomena is likewise thus; being free from existence and non-existence, one should not form conceptualizations regarding them. Mahāmati!
Furthermore, if one forms the notion that a rabbit has no horns while departing from both existence and non-existence, this is called a false conception (*mithyā-saṃjñā*).

Since the absence of horns in a rabbit must be understood through dependent observation, one should not form such a conception; even down to the subtlest atom, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be apprehended through discrimination.
"Mahāmati! Since the realm of the noble ones is free from [dualistic extremes], one should not form the conceptualization that 'cows have horns.

Those non-Buddhists give rise to the two views of existence and non-existence because they do not understand that all phenomena are mind-only; they merely increase their delusive conceptualizations and discriminations regarding the objects of their own minds."
As for the worldly requisites for sustaining the body, none are anything other than the measure of the deluded mind.
The sense organs (*indriya*) are, in essence, the mind itself.
If one can penetrate this measure of the mind, one will realize that all manifested realms are illusory, and the dualistic views of existence and non-existence will thereby be extinguished.

He further addressed Mahāmati: "Not only are mental phenomena fundamentally empty, but the nature of all dharmas is likewise fundamentally free from the characteristics of existence and non-existence; one should not engage in false conceptualization."
Furthermore, if one claims to be free from both existence and non-existence by forming the notion that a rabbit has no horns, this too is a false conception.

Regarding the phrase "dependent upon contemplation," "dependent" means "in relation to. This refers to the existence of the cow's horn being observed in contrast to the non-existence of the rabbit's horn; since this is not true emptiness, it says, "one should not form such a notion."
As for the intrinsic nature of atoms, their substance and characteristics cannot be found upon investigation.
This is because the realm of noble wisdom is fundamentally free from such views; therefore, one should not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding this.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

regarding those who have attained freedom from false conceptualization, having perceived the characteristic of non-arising, do they, in accordance with their deliberation and observation, declare that conceptualization is non-existent because it does not arise?”
Having thus refuted that the "existence" and "non-existence" of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are neither correct causes, he asked again:

"Now, in the True Teaching, those who have attained freedom from deluded thoughts see only the characteristic of non-arising; how does this differ from the non-Buddhists' observation of the non-arising of deluded thoughts and their assertion of 'non-existence'?"
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"It is not because of the non-arising of conceptualization through investigation that one says 'non-existent. Why is this so?"
Regarding "false conceptualization" (*vikalpa*): because it arises dependent upon that [horn], false conceptualization arises based on that horn.

Since false conceptualization arises based on the horn, it is said to arise from a cause; and because it is neither different nor non-different [from its object], one does not say that the horn is non-existent simply because false conceptualization does not arise when one does not examine [the object].

In response, the initial clarification of what is not [the case] states that it is "not an observation" and so forth; this is because one realizes that deluded thoughts lack intrinsic nature and are thus non-existent, which differs from the conceptualization that speaks of non-existence in contrast to existence.

In essence, he regards discriminative conceptualization as the cause for the arising of phenomena; just as one gives rise to discrimination based on whether a horn exists or not, it is therefore said: "Because one relies upon the horn, conceptualization arises."

Regarding the statement "neither different nor non-different": "different" refers to the arising of the conceptual discrimination of existence and non-existence based on the horn; "non-different" refers to the absence of such conceptualization regarding the horn.
Because one is free from these views, it is said: "It is not through investigation that one gives rise to the false imagination and says there is no horn."
“Mahāmati! If, furthermore, the false imagination were different from the horns, then it would not arise from the horns.

If it were not different, then because it depends upon them—even when analyzed and sought down to the level of atoms—it would be entirely unfindable; since it is not different from the horns, it too lacks intrinsic nature.”
Regarding the absence of nature in both: what dharma and for what reason do you say it is non-existent? Mahāmati!
If one says that because [the cow] is absent the horn is non-existent, and observes its presence to say that the rabbit has no horns, such a conceptualization should not be made.
"Mahāmati! Because of incorrect causes, both existence and non-existence are equally unestablished.
This further statement—that "discrimination is different from horns and so forth"—is a re-explanation of the aforementioned meaning.
If one claims that conceptual construction is different from the horn, then the horn would not be the causal basis [of that construction].

If they are not different, then since conceptual construction arises based upon it, and yet when analyzed down to the level of atoms, neither is to be found, then both views—existence and non-existence of the horn—are extinguished. Therefore, it is said: "Because it is not different from the horn, it also lacks intrinsic nature."
"Non-nature" (*abhāva*) means it is not a real nature.
If both existence and non-existence were devoid of nature, with respect to what phenomenon would one speak of "non-existence"?

To say that horns do not exist because they are non-existent implies that the absence of horns is distinct from the presence of horns; such a principle is absolutely untenable, and therefore it is said that one should not form such a conceptualization.

Regarding the term "incorrect reasons," it means that those who fail to obtain correct reasons for establishing existence or non-existence lack any real meaning; therefore, it is said, "both are unestablished."

“Mahāmati! Furthermore, there are other views held by non-Buddhists who, being attached to the emptiness of matter, its objects, shapes, and spatial dimensions, fail to properly understand the limits of space. They claim that matter is separate from space, thereby giving rise to the false discrimination of views regarding spatial boundaries.”
He again raises the externalist view regarding the meaning of the emptiness of form (*rūpa-śūnyatā*) to refute its cause, as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*:

"Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who, seeing the shapes and boundaries of form within space, give rise to attachment; they claim that form is distinct from space, thereby giving rise to conceptual discrimination."
“Mahāmati! Space is that which enters into form according to the categories of form. Mahāmati!”
Form is established as the locus of that which is held by space; one should understand that it is the nature of form and the activity of emptiness that are thus distinguished.
Mahāmati! When the four great elements arise, their self-characteristics are each distinct; they do not abide in space, yet it is not that space does not exist therein.
The former statement spoke of the improper discrimination between form and emptiness; this statement says that emptiness is form and form is emptiness.

Regarding "the holder and that which is held": it means that form is supported by space, and within that which is supported, all forms are established. Thus, there is no form outside of emptiness; they function as both subject and object to one another.
How can it be said that one is free from the view of establishing boundaries based on space?
As for the statement regarding "the nature of form and emptiness," this refers to the matter of the nature of form and the nature of emptiness; it should be distinguished in this manner.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"The demarcation between form and emptiness should be understood in this way.
As for the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), they are earth, water, fire, and wind.

When these four great elements arise, their specific characteristics—solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion—are each distinct; although they do not abide within space, they have never been separate from it. Therefore, it is said: "Without them, there is no space."
"In this way, Mahāmati!
Because one observes that the ox has horns, one concludes that the rabbit has no horns. Mahāmati!"
Furthermore, if one analyzes a cow's horn into atoms, and further analyzes those atoms as not abiding for even a single moment, what is there to be observed that one could say does not exist?
If you claim that it is other things that are being observed, then those phenomena are likewise [subject to the same analysis].
Regarding the observation that "the ox has horns" and so forth, this is stated in contrast to the existence of the ox's horn to express the non-existence of the rabbit's horn.

If this ox's horn is analyzed into atoms, and further divided and subdivided until reaching the *paramāṇu* (infinitesimal particle), then its perceived characteristic of being perceived vanishes; even seeking its characteristic of momentary duration, it cannot be found.
A "kṣaṇa" (moment) is a subtle thought-instant.
When those non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) calculate that something is "non-existent," they do so in contrast to the existence of a cow's horn.
Since not even a single atom of a cow's horn can be found when sought, one must ask: in contrast to what object do they claim it is non-existent?
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:
"If it depends on another thing, that [other thing] is likewise so.
Here, "depends" (*dai*) means "in relation to" (*dui*).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying:

“You should abandon the false conceptualizations of differences in views regarding rabbit horns, cow horns, space, and form-and-color. You, all you Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas, should contemplate the false conceptualizations manifested by your own minds; entering accordingly as the most excellent sons of all buddha-lands, you should instruct them through the skillful means of what is manifested by your own minds.”
This passage exhorts one to abandon two kinds of views.

Furthermore, it says: "One should contemplate that false discrimination is a manifestation of one's own mind. Desiring to know the reality of whether false discrimination exists or does not exist, one should simply look back at one's own mind and ask: is it ultimately existent, or is it ultimately non-existent?
"Is it both existent and non-existent, or neither existent nor non-existent?
Reflect upon this and you will understand it for yourself.
You should likewise instruct others in this manner; therefore, it is said: 'Entering accordingly into all buddha-fields.'"
"O Son of the Most Victorious One, you are indeed a son of the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The aggregates such as form and the mind do not exist; The aggregates such as form nourish the mind."
The body, its enjoyments, and their establishment, The storehouse consciousness appearing as sentient beings;
Mind, mentation, and consciousness, The five dharmas of intrinsic nature,
And the two kinds of selflessness and purity— Thus has the Proclaimer extensively taught.
Length, shortness, existence, non-existence, and so forth—these arise from one another in mutual succession.
Because of non-existence, existence is established; because of existence, non-existence is established.
By analytically discerning atoms, one does not give rise to the false conceptualization of form.
The locus established by mind-only is not what those with evil views delight in;
it is not the sphere of discursive thought, nor is it for the śrāvakas.
This is what the Savior has taught: the sphere of self-realization.

Regarding the statement that "form and so forth, as well as mind, do not exist": this means that the aforementioned imagined nature does not emerge apart from external objects such as form and internal consciousness-mind.
According to reason, these have fundamentally never existed.
This single word "No" is a sharp blade for severing delusions; nothing surpasses it. If you can take this up and bear it, what thought would not be eliminated?

It is only because ordinary people do not understand that they give rise to deluded thoughts, and instead take these very thoughts to nourish their own minds; thus, the body, its enjoyments, and all other things are established thereby.
Speaking from the perspective of the fundamental source, because they are manifestations of the *ālayavijñāna*, mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) arise in succession.

Regarding the five factors of self-nature (*svabhāva-dharma*), these are established by way of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) as the five dharmas—name (*nāma*) and so forth—and the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*).
Regarding the phrase "explained at length," the verse states that the conceptualization of existence and non-existence, as well as relative dependence (*apekṣā*), are all not the correct causes.

The statement that "the analysis of atoms does not give rise to form and so forth" refers to the verse's analysis of horns and the absence of horns; these are false conceptualizations and deluded imaginings.

Regarding the "establishment of the scope of mind" (*cittamātra-vyavasthāna*): the verse above contemplates one's own mind as being free from the conceptualizations of existence and non-existence; this is precisely the locus of establishment for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). It is not an object of delight for the perceptions and imaginings of the heterodox or the inferior views of the *Hīnayāna*, but rather the realm of self-realization (*pratyātma-gati*) taught by the Buddha.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva, in order to purify the stream of manifestations within his own mind, again requested the Tathāgata,
saying to the Buddha: "World-Honored One,
how does one purify the stream of manifestations within the minds of all sentient beings— is it sudden or gradual?"

The "stream of what is manifested by one's own mind" refers to the continuous flow of afflictions arising from the activity of the eight consciousnesses as manifestations of one's own mind; it is also called the habitual tendencies of the faults manifested by one's own mind.
Mahāmati asked for the method to purify [the mind], inquiring whether it was sudden or gradual.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Purification is gradual, not sudden."

Just as the mango fruit ripens gradually and not all at once, so too does the Tathāgata purify the stream of mental manifestations within the minds of all sentient beings; this purification is gradual and not instantaneous.

For example, when a potter fashions various vessels, they are completed gradually rather than instantaneously; likewise, the Tathāgata’s purification of the stream of mental manifestations within the minds of all sentient beings is also gradual, not instantaneous.

Just as the great earth gradually gives rise to the myriad things rather than producing them all at once, so too does the Tathāgata purify the stream of mental manifestations within the minds of all sentient beings; this purification is gradual, not instantaneous.

For example, when a person learns music, writing, painting, and various other arts and crafts, they are accomplished gradually and not instantaneously; likewise, the Tathāgata’s purification of the stream of mental manifestations within the minds of all sentient beings is also gradual and not instantaneous.

Just as a bright mirror suddenly manifests all forms and images that are devoid of marks, so too does the Tathāgata purify the stream of manifestations from the minds of all sentient beings; he suddenly manifests the markless, which is a pure realm where nothing whatsoever exists.

Just as the orbs of the sun and moon suddenly illuminate and reveal all forms and images, so too does the Tathāgata, for the sake of sentient beings who have not yet abandoned the faults of the habitual tendencies arising from their own minds, suddenly reveal the supreme realm of inconceivable wisdom.

For example, just as the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) instantaneously discerns and knows the manifestations of its own mind, as well as the establishment of the body and the objects of experience, so too do those Buddhas of the Support (āśrayabuddha); they instantaneously mature the realms where sentient beings dwell, establishing practitioners in that Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

Just as the light emitted by the *nirmāṇakāya* (the Buddha of manifestation) produced by the *dharmakāya* (the Buddha of reality) shines forth, so too is the noble path of self-realization; it illuminates and causes the extinction of the evil views and false imaginings regarding the existence or non-existence of the nature of phenomena.
This section demonstrates the characteristics of gradual and sudden purification.

From the passage where the Buddha addresses Mahāmati onwards, the characteristics of gradual purification are shown; there are four analogies in total, each consisting of the principle (*dharma*), the analogy (*upamā*), and the application (*upanaya*), all of which can be seen in the text.
Below the passage "For example, as in a bright mirror," four further metaphors are presented to illustrate the aspect of sudden purity.

First, regarding "images of forms that are non-existent": these are images within the brightness itself; the substance of the image is fundamentally empty. This serves as a metaphor for the fact that within the Dharma, the realm of signlessness is fundamentally non-existent; therefore, it is said, "there is nothing that exists."

Regarding the analogy for the *ālayavijñāna* that speaks of "simultaneous discerning cognition," this does not mean that the *ālayavijñāna* itself performs the discernment; rather, it refers to the discernment of the objects manifested by the *ālayavijñāna*.
It is like a mirror manifesting images. This analogy is based on the realm inhabited by sentient beings of great faculties who have been suddenly matured by the Buddha.
Regarding the term "dependent Buddha" (*nirmāṇakāya-buddha*), it refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha, because the *saṃbhogakāya* relies upon the *dharmakāya*.

Regarding the phrase "for example, the dependent Buddha produced by the *dharmakāya* Buddha," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "For example, the *dharmakāya* Buddha suddenly manifests the *saṃbhogakāya* and the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddhas. This is what is meant.
"The noble path of self-realization" refers to the personally realized realm of the noble ones.
It is that which illuminates and causes the extinction of the evil views of outsiders who cling to the nature of existence and non-existence. "Mahāmati!..."

The Dharma, as taught by the Buddha, states that all phenomena enter into their own-characteristics and common characteristics; they have the habitual tendencies of what is manifested by one's own mind as their cause, and the attachment to the self-nature of continuous false discrimination as their cause. They are manifold and unreal like illusions; manifold attachments cannot be found.

Regarding "the Dharma-reliant Buddha": "Dharma" refers to the Dharmakāya, while the "reliant Buddha" refers to the function of the Sambhogakāya; this means that the entire essence gives rise to its function to expound all dharmas, wherein "Dharma" refers specifically to the Mahāyāna Dharma.

Regarding "entering into the grasping of specific and general characteristics": it means that sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamental nature and enter into the grasping of specific and general characteristics; these are afflictions manifested by one's own mind, termed the cause of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Due to the continuity of afflictions (*kleśa*), one falsely conceives and creates various karmic bonds; this is called the "cause of attachment.
Because one undergoes all manner of false birth and death due to these afflictions and karmic bonds, it is said that they are "unreal, like an illusion."
These three paths encompass the nine realms; hence it is said, "various attachments. However, these three paths are fundamentally the Three Virtues (triguṇa).

Sentient beings, deluded by them, transmigrate through the three paths. The Buddha teaches this Dharma so that they may realize that their own nature is originally empty—transforming the false into the true, such that both truth and falsehood are extinguished. Therefore, it is said that they are "unattainable."
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
by clinging to the dependent origination of self-nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) arise. Mahāmati!"

It is like a master illusionist who, relying on grass, wood, tiles, and stones, creates various illusions, manifesting the diverse forms and colors of all sentient beings and giving rise to various false conceptions; yet those false conceptions possess no reality whatsoever.

These words mean that all phenomena, such as the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), do not transcend two kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). Since the characteristic of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) arises from the dependent origination nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), he further clarifies this by means of a simile.
Performing various illusions based on grass, wood, and so forth is a metaphor for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
As for "forms, colors, and so forth," this refers to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Those various delusions are like the illusory forms created by a magician; therefore, it is said that "they also lack reality.
"In this way, Mahāmati!

Based on the dependent origination-nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) arises. This includes the various deluded minds, the various characteristics and activities of the deluded mind, and the delusion of attachment to habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); this is what constitutes the manifestation of the imagined nature."
"Mahāmati! This is called the teaching of the Dharma by the *dharmatā-niṣyanda-buddha* (the Buddha of natural outflow).
Previously, the various false conceptualizations were illustrated through the analogy of illusion; here, that previous analogy is applied.

Regarding the phrase "various deluded thoughts, mind, and so forth": because there is mind, there is perception; because there is perception, there is volitional formation; because there is volitional formation, there is phenomena. There is nothing that is not deluded thought.
These are precisely the characteristics of the three preceding natures; they differ only in their expansion and contraction.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"Due to the power of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from clinging to objects, various characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) appear within the dependent origination nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); this is called the arising of the imagined nature."
Since the meaning is clear, I have cited the commentary here; this is called the conclusion regarding the Buddha’s teaching based on the Dharma.

“Mahāmati, the Dharma-Buddha is free from the self-nature and characteristics of the mind; it is established and enacted as the objective realm perceived by the noble ones through their own self-realization.”
The Dharma-Buddha is the Dharma-body cultivated through merit.
To say that it is "separated from the self-nature and characteristics of the mind" means to be separated from deluded thoughts.
Furthermore, since the Dharma-body is ultimate, what is there that it does not transcend?
The reason for specifically mentioning the "mind" is that the mind is the root of all phenomena; if the mind does not perish, then all phenomena arise.
Now, when one speaks of being "detached from marks," it means that all phenomena are quiescent and extinguished.
The characteristic of quiescent extinction refers to the Dharma-body.
Since it is said to be "devoid of characteristics," how could the name or characteristics of the Dharma-body be established?
Therefore, it is said: "It is established and enacted as the objective realm perceived by the noble ones' self-awakening."
What is meant by this? To insist on designating *dharmatā* as the *dharmakāya* is to speak of a name that has no name, a characteristic that has no characteristic. "Mahāmati!

The *nirmāṇa-buddha* teaches giving, the elements (*dhātu*), patience, vigor, meditative concentration, as well as mind and wisdom; it is free from the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, from liberation, and from the conceptual discrimination of the characteristics of consciousness; it establishes [the path] through observation and transcends the views of non-Buddhists and the views of the formless."
The "Transformation Buddha" (nirmāṇakāya-buddha) is precisely the Response Body Buddha (nirmāṇakāya), who preaches the Dharma of the Three Vehicles to deliver all sentient beings.

The Six Perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) that he teaches are the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas, which is free from the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), the eighteen elements (aṣṭādaśa-dhātu), the twelve bases (dvādaśāyatana), and even liberation (vimukti).
The differentiation of the characteristics of consciousness refers to the teachings of the Two Vehicles.

"Observation and establishment" refers to the meaning of the two kinds of awakening mentioned later in the text; these constitute the methods for a bodhisattva’s self-cultivation and the transformation of others.
"Transcending the views of external paths" means being free from the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.
"The view of formlessness" refers to reckoning the meditative absorption of formlessness as the definitive state of nirvana, which is the cessation of sensation, perception, and consciousness.
“Mahāmati! Furthermore, the Dharma-Buddha is free from objective reference (*ālambana*).

Being free from objective reference, all activities, faculties, means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and marks are extinguished. This is not the realm of attachment for ordinary people, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or non-Buddhists who cling to the mark of a self; rather, it is established as the ultimate, distinguished characteristic of the noble ones’ personal realization.”
"Therefore, Mahāmati,

you should diligently cultivate and study the distinctive characteristics of the ultimate realization of the noble self-awakened ones, and you should eliminate the perception of what is manifested by one's own mind.
Furthermore, regarding the Dharma-Buddha, this is a reiterated instruction on that which is to be abandoned.
The preceding statement regarding "separation from the mind" refers to the separation from its own essence (*svabhāva*).
Now, by further demonstrating "separation," it refers to the separation from the objects of separation.

To be separated from objective conditions (*ālambana*) distinguishes one from ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); to be separated from both objective conditions and [subjective] clinging distinguishes one from those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
In short, although the followers of the Two Vehicles have detached themselves from external objects, they remain attached to emptiness; the Buddha, however, is not so.

That all conditioned activities and the characteristics of the sense-bases and their objects are extinguished distinguishes him from the non-Buddhists; therefore it is said: "It is not the realm of attachment for ordinary beings, nor even for those [of the Two Vehicles]."
Since that which is transcended is ultimate, it is nothing other than the realm of self-awakened sages.

As for what is called the "ultimate differentiated characteristic," "ultimate" refers to the limit of the stage of fruition (*phala*), while "differentiated" refers to differentiation by means of unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*); it is a differentiation that is without difference.
There are two concluding exhortations:
the first exhorts practice and study, concluding the current section of the text;
the second concerns eradication, concluding the preceding discussion on the flow of what is manifested within one's own mind.

"Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of general characteristics of the Śrāvaka vehicle: namely, the characteristic of the distinction of the noble self-realization, and the characteristic of attachment to the imagined nature of intrinsic being."
What is the śrāvaka who attains the distinctive characteristics of self-realized noble wisdom?

It refers to one who, regarding the spheres of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, realizes the truth of detachment, cessation, and the stilling of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; who knows as they truly are the internal and external non-disintegrating characteristics, and whose mind attains tranquil abiding.

Once the mind has attained tranquility, there is the meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), samādhi, the fruits of the path, and the meditative attainments and liberations; yet, because they have not abandoned habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and the inconceivable death of transformation (*pariṇāmiki-cyuti*), they abide in the noble bliss of self-realization as śrāvakas. These are called śrāvakas who have attained the distinctive characteristics of the noble state of self-realization.

"Since there are differences in the magnitude of the noble wisdom cultivated by Bodhisattvas as they strive for self-awakening, there are two distinct types of characteristics that emerge from what is realized by Śrāvakas:
first, the characteristic of the distinction of the noble self-awakening, which refers to the principle realized;
second, the characteristic of attachment to the self-nature of false conceptualization, which refers to the arising of views based on clinging to the teachings."
Although they are equally śrāvakas, their gains and losses differ eternally.
Impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self refer to the śrāvaka’s cultivation of the contemplation of analytical emptiness.
"Realm" refers to the object that is empty.
"Ultimate Truth" refers to the true principle.
"Detachment from desire and tranquil extinction" refers to departing from the cravings of the three realms and entering the nirvana without remainder.

The cessation of the five aggregates (*skandha*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and the twelve bases (*āyatana*)—both their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), their common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and their combined specific and common characteristics—is what constitutes the "general and particular characteristics.

Regarding the phrase "knowing the external non-disintegrating characteristic as it truly is": this means that the Śrāvakas cannot, as it truly is, realize that the characteristic of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is identical to the characteristic of nirvāṇa; therefore, they regard it as "external. Because they must attain quiescent extinction (*śānti*) before their minds can cease, and because their minds have ceased and become tranquil, they attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) up to the correct reception (*samāpatti*) and liberation (*vimukti*).

Regarding the phrase "not being free from habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)": the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be eliminated consist of both the manifest (*maula*) and the habitual. One can only sever the manifest, thereby leaving behind the death-and-rebirth of the fragmented existence (*prādeśika-jarāmaraṇa*);
yet, as one has not yet severed the habitual, there still remains the death-and-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*).
"Segmented" refers to the segmented birth and death within the three realms, characterized by physical form and duration.
"Transformative" refers to the birth and death in the land of skillful means, wherein the cause shifts and the fruit changes.
Regarding the term "inconceivable," this refers to the death and rebirth through transformation (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*), which is beyond the capacity of ordinary beings to conceive.
Regarding "delighting in dwelling," this refers to the śrāvakas delighting in dwelling within the nirvāṇa of true emptiness.

“Mahāmati! The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who has attained the distinguished dwelling in the bliss of self-realized noble wisdom does not realize the bliss of the gate of cessation or the bliss of meditative absorption; out of compassion for sentient beings and due to his original vows, he does not bring about such realization.”
“Mahāmati! This is called the pleasure of the distinctive characteristics of the noble self-realization attained by the śrāvakas.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not train in that pleasure of the distinctive characteristics of the noble self-realization.”
This means that the Bodhisattva also realizes the ultimate truth yet does not dwell in or cling to it.

Regarding the statement "not the gate of cessation," this is unlike the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which dwells in the gate of quiescent extinction and proceeds toward the bliss of meditative absorption.

Regarding the phrase "looking back with compassion for sentient beings" and so forth, it means that a bodhisattva delivers beings through the power of compassionate vows and does not cling to nirvana.
This is a further summary indicating that while this is the bliss of the samādhi attained by śrāvakas, a bodhisattva should not practice or study such samādhi.
“Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of the attachment to the imagined nature of the mind of the śrāvaka? It is as follows:

having seen that the great elements—blue, yellow, red, white, solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion—are produced without a creator, and having heard the excellent teachings on their specific and general characteristics by those who were formerly superior, they give rise to the imagination of an intrinsic nature regarding them.”

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should know and abandon those [characteristics], entering into accordance with the characteristic of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), extinguishing the views regarding the characteristic of the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), and gradually establishing the continuity of the various stages (*bhūmi*). This is called the characteristic of attachment to the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*) of the nature of the śrāvakas.
This section investigates and explains the śrāvakas who cling to signs.

First, it explains the delusion regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*): it asserts that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) each possess an inherent nature (*svabhāva*). For instance, earth has solidity as its nature, water has moisture as its nature, fire has warmth as its nature, and wind has motion as its nature.

Regarding the phrase "arising without being made," it means arising without being produced through volitional construction; nevertheless, one still gives rise to attachment toward the individual and common characteristics of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas).

[The opponent claims: "The former victors were Buddhas, meaning that the Buddhas skillfully proclaimed that the śrāvakas who cling to the sounds of the teachings cannot realize that self-nature is fundamentally empty; seeing the various marks within those realms, they give rise to conceptualizations of self-nature."
A bodhisattva should recognize these faults and abandon them, entering accordingly into the characteristics of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
As the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:
"Having departed from the view of the selflessness of persons, one enters the characteristics of the selflessness of phenomena and gradually ascends through the stages (*bhūmi*)."
This concludes the section on the "Lower.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"World-Honored One, regarding the realm of the self-realized noble path and the realm of the ultimate truth— which You describe as eternal and inconceivable— is this not, World-Honored One,
the same 'eternal and inconceivable cause' taught by the non-Buddhists?"

The Tathāgata’s discourse on the eternal and inconceivable shares the same terminology as that spoken by non-Buddhists; fearing that students might confuse the authentic with the false and fall into delusion, he raises this as a question.
The names are identical but the meanings differ, as will be fully seen in the following text.
What are termed "the eternal" and "the inconceivable" do not transcend two kinds of realms:
the eternal refers to the noble path of self-awakening, while the inconceivable refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Self-awakening is the eternal wisdom;
the noble realm is the eternal object.
Because one accords with the eternal object by means of eternal wisdom, it is called "eternal."
The essence of the ultimate truth transcends speech and thought; therefore, it is called "inconceivable.
How could it ever be the same as the false views of non-Buddhists?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"The eternal and inconceivable is not attained through the causal conditions of the non-Buddhists. Why is this?
Because the eternal and inconceivable of the non-Buddhists is not established by means of their own characteristics."
If the eternal and inconceivable were not established by way of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), for what reason would it manifest as eternal and inconceivable?
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
if the inconceivable were established by way of its own characteristic, then it would necessarily be eternal.
"Because it possesses the characteristics of being produced by a creator, it cannot be established as eternal or inconceivable.

The response, "This is not like the causal conditions of the non-Buddhists," implies that the cultivation and realization of the non-Buddhists do not rely on correct causes and conditions; since their causes are not correct causes and their results are not correct results, he interrogates, explains, and thereby refutes them.

That which is not established by way of its own-characteristic means that it is not accomplished through the characteristic of self-awareness; in that case, the fruit—the realm of the eternal and inconceivable—would likewise not be established.
If that cause were established from the characteristic of self-awareness, then because the cause is eternal, the fruit would also be eternal.

Regarding the phrase "due to the cause of activity and characteristics," it is because the cause that produces [the result] is a false conceptualization; therefore, the eternal and inconceivable does not achieve fruition. "Mahāmati!..."

My ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is eternal and inconceivable; it is established through the characteristics of the cause of ultimate reality. It possesses characteristics because it attains the characteristic of self-realization, being free from both existence and non-existence. It possesses causes because it is the cause for the wisdom of ultimate reality, as it is free from both existence and non-existence.
For example, like unconditioned space, nirvana is eternal because it is the cessation of all things.
In this way, Mahāmati,
it is not the same as the non-Buddhists' doctrine of an eternal and inconceivable [self].
Thus it is, Mahāmati!

This permanence and inconceivability are attained through the noble wisdom of self-realization by all Tathāgatas; therefore, one should practice and study that which is attained through the noble wisdom of self-realization, which is permanent and inconceivable.

This refutes the errors of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) and reveals the correctness of the True Teaching. Regarding the statement that "the primary meaning (paramārtha) is established through causes and characteristics," this primary meaning is precisely the Middle Way and the true nature of reality (dharmatā).

To take this as the cause is to have a permanent cause; to take this as the characteristic is to have a permanent characteristic. It is far removed from the faults of existence and non-existence: to be free from "nature" (svabhāva) means it is not existent; to be free from "non-nature" (asvabhāva) means it is not non-existent. Being neither existent nor non-existent correctly manifests the Middle Way. Because the Middle Way is beyond all relative dependence, it is eternal; because it is eternal, it is sublime; because it is sublime, it is inconceivable. This is why it is thus ultimately eternal and inconceivable. Since it differs from those non-Buddhists who lack a cause with its own specific characteristic, it is further stated that there is a cause and there are characteristics.

Regarding the statement "for example, like non-action, space, and so forth": space is eternal because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and nirvāṇa is eternal because it is the cessation of all things. This eternity that is inconceivable is not at all comparable to the contentious arguments of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Regarding the phrase "all Tathāgatas and so forth," the Buddha said: "It is not only my Dharma that is thus; that which all Buddhas have realized—the eternal and inconceivable—is likewise always so."
Therefore, it is enjoined that a bodhisattva should practice and study this.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the permanence and inconceivability of the non-Buddhists' notion of impermanence is due to the cause of dissimilar characteristics; it is not permanent by virtue of the power of its own causal characteristics.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!

The various non-Buddhists, having perceived that the nature of what is produced is neither existent nor non-existent and is impermanent, then through deliberation and calculation, they conceive it to be eternal.

This passage refutes the reason why the non-Buddhists' notion of impermanence is invalid, challenging their lack of result because their cause is not a true cause; it further refutes them by repeatedly addressing the nature of that cause.
As for what is called a "cause of dissimilar characteristics," it is not the characteristic of my own self-cause.

That which they call "permanent" is not a permanence established by the power of the true reality of its own correct cause; rather, it is a permanence that consists of misapprehending the impermanent as permanent. How could such a thing manifest the fruit of the nature of permanence?

Furthermore, regarding that which non-Buddhists conceive as eternal and inconceivable, they say: "The phenomena produced in the world exist and then cease to exist; all are impermanent, for 'nature' and 'non-nature' are simply existence and non-existence."
Having formed such a view, one falsely conceives of a self (ātman) as being eternal and inconceivable; therefore, it is said that "one deliberates and reckons it as eternal. "Mahāmati!..."

I, too, having perceived through such causes and conditions that the nature of what is created is neither existence nor non-existence and is characterized by impermanence, speak of that permanence as being without cause within the realm of the self-realized noble ones.

Mahāmati! Furthermore, if the various non-Buddhists establish permanence and inconceivability based on causal characteristics, their causal self-characteristics—whether existent or non-existent—are identical to the horns of a rabbit; this permanence and inconceivability are merely verbal conceptualizations.
The various non-Buddhist schools fall into such errors.
Why is this? It is because their mere verbal conceptualizations are like the horns of a rabbit; they do not pertain to the characteristics of their own causes.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "I am also thus through causes and conditions," it means that the Tathāgata likewise perceives that nature to be impermanent yet cultivates the perception of permanence; having manifested the realm of the noble self-realization, he subsequently knows that nature to be impermanent, and therefore speaks of its permanence as being without cause.

Furthermore, if one were to establish the eternal and inconceivable through the false causes and false characteristics of non-Buddhists, such a cause would possess only a self-characteristic in name but lack any real meaning; therefore, it is said to be "the same as a rabbit's horn."
The section beginning with "The various heterodox practitioners" concludes the refutation of their errors, which are briefly summarized as fourfold:

first, the conceptualization of verbal expression; second, the improper attribution of self-causality to phenomena; third, the failure to realize the nature of things through self-awakening; and fourth, the speculative reckoning of permanence. Therefore, it is said: "There are such errors."

“Mahāmati! Because my eternal and inconceivable cause is realized through self-awakening as having its own characteristic, it is eternal because it is free from the nature of being produced and because it is not a [mere] non-nature; it is not the impermanence of external natures or non-natures, which is merely a constant based on deliberation and calculation.”

Mahāmati! If, moreover, external natures—whether existent or non-existent—are impermanent, yet one speculates and calculates them to be permanent or inconceivably permanent, and fails to understand the characteristics of the self-cause of that permanence and inconceivability, then such a person is far removed from the characteristics of the realm of self-realized noble wisdom and should not speak [of these matters].

Regarding the phrase "I am always inconceivable," etc., the Buddha states that what I have attained is inconceivable; taking self-realization as its causal characteristic, it differs from the non-Buddhists who hold that things exist and then cease to exist, making them impermanent, or who use the concept of a *puruṣa* (self) to calculate and conceive of permanence.
Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, as for external nature," etc., this again refutes externalist calculations through four points:

first, it refutes the calculation based on deliberation that [the world] is eternal; second, it is called "not knowing the characteristics of the self-cause of the inconceivable eternal"; third, it refutes being far removed from the characteristics attained by the Buddha; and fourth, the phrase "they should not speak" refutes their having nothing but mere verbal expressions.

"Furthermore, Mahāmati, the śrāvakas, fearing the suffering of the conceptualization of birth-and-death, seek nirvāṇa; they do not know that the distinction between birth-and-death and nirvāṇa consists in the fact that all natures are non-natures due to conceptualization."

When the future sense-faculties and their objects cease, one conceives the notion of nirvana; however, this is not the transformation of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) through the noble wisdom of self-realization. For this reason, the foolish proclaim the existence of three vehicles and speak of the mind-only as tending toward non-existence.
Therefore, Mahāmati!

Because they do not understand that the realms of the past, future, and present Tathāgatas are the manifestations of their own minds, they cling to external realms manifested by the mind; thus, the wheel of birth and death revolves eternally.

Those of the Hīnayāna fear birth and death and long for nirvāṇa, yet they do not know that the distinct characteristics of birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are all merely false imaginings and possess no real nature.

The wisdom-eye of this Hīnayāna perceives the cessation of future faculties and sense-objects and takes this to be *nirvāṇa*; how could this truly be the realm reached by the noble wisdom of self-realization?
Nor is it the nirvana that is manifested by the ālayavijñāna.

As for what is called the teaching of the three vehicles by the ignorant and deluded: they do not understand the Mahāyāna dharma that birth-and-death is itself nirvana; therefore, for their sake, the emptiness of the small vehicle's nirvana is taught.
That the measure of the mind is non-existent is itself true emptiness.

Yet, one does not realize that the wondrous mind of nirvana of the Buddhas of the three periods of time is manifested from one's own mind and is not something separate; instead, one falsely discriminates that there are dharmas external to the mind, giving rise to delusion and creating karma, thereby revolving through birth and death.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
That 'all dharmas are unarisen' is what has been taught by all Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present. Why is this so?
This means that the nature of what is manifested by one's own mind is neither existent nor non-existent, because it is free from birth as either existence or non-existence. Mahāmati!
All natures are unborn; all phenomena are like the horns of rabbits or horses, yet ignorant ordinary people do not realize that they are merely the false imaginings of the self-nature of delusion.

Mahāmati! Regarding the fact that all dharmas are unborn and that the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization is entered: it is because the characteristics of the self-nature of all entities are unborn; it is not the dualistic realm of the false imaginings of those foolish people, nor is it the establishment of the self-nature of the body and its possessions as a realm of self-nature.

Mahāmati! The ālayavijñāna evolves through the characteristics of grasping and being grasped; foolish people fall into the dualistic views of arising, abiding, and ceasing, hoping for the birth of all natures, and giving rise to the false discrimination of existence and non-existence—this is not the way of the noble ones.
"Mahāmati! You should practice and study therein.
If even non-arising cannot be found when sought within the portions of the Buddhas, how much less so can all dharmas?
It is precisely because sentient beings have been attached to all phenomena since beginningless time that the Buddhas shatter their former calculations and thus speak of "non-arising.
Since all phenomena are merely manifestations of one's own mind and lack any intrinsic nature, how could they not be devoid of arising?
It is also free from non-arising;
this is what the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* refers to as "the non-arising of non-arising.

Regarding the phrase "all natures are non-arising" and so forth, this is further presented in terms of delusion and enlightenment to demonstrate gain and loss. It means that one cannot realize that arising is itself non-arising, but merely says that all natures are non-arising. To conceptualize and cling to all phenomena as being like the horns of a rabbit or a horse is because these fools do not awaken to the fact that their own deluded thoughts are themselves the delusions of self-nature; it is not the "non-arising" spoken of here.

If it is said that all dharmas are non-arising—that which is the sphere of the noble wisdom of the Tathāgata’s self-realization—then the nature and characteristics of all dharmas are both non-arising; this is true non-arising, not the dualistic objects of existence and non-existence as conceptualized by the deluded thoughts of foolish people.
Regarding the phrase "the self-nature body, its provisions, and so forth," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"The body, the requisites for life, the vessel-world, and all else are entirely images of the ālayavijñāna, appearing as the two aspects of the grasped and the grasper."

Fools do not understand this; they fall into the dualistic views of arising, abiding, and ceasing, or existence and non-existence. They grasp at the arising of all natures and fail to transcend the false imaginings of existence and non-existence. In truth, that which is called "non-arising" is not something attained by ordinary beings; it is what is realized by the noble ones.
Regarding the phrase "in that regard," one should practice and study the non-arising taught by all Buddhas.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are five lineages of immediate succession.
What are these five? They are:

the lineage of immediate succession for the Śrāvaka vehicle, the lineage of immediate succession for the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, the lineage of immediate succession for the Tathāgata vehicle, the indeterminate lineage, and the distinct lineage.

Regarding their spiritual lineage (*gotra*), there is fundamentally no distinction; yet, due to beginningless habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), it may be internal or external, great or small, fixed or unfixed.

The reason this sutra clarifies that there are five types of spiritual lineage (*gotra*) by using the term "uninterrupted" (*anantara*) is that their lineage is pure, singular, and free from admixture.
How is it known that one possesses the uninterrupted lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle?

If, upon hearing it said that the self-characteristics and common characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are to be abandoned through knowledge, one’s every pore becomes radiant with joy and delight, and one delights in cultivating the wisdom of signs while failing to cultivate the signs of awakening through dependent origination, this is called the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle of immediate succession.

The śrāvaka perceives the eighth stage without interval; while he has severed the active afflictions (*kleśa*), he has not yet severed the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*). He has not transcended the inconceivable death of transformation (*nirmita-vaiparītya-maraṇa*), but he has transcended the death of fragmentation (*bhedana-maraṇa*). He rightly roars the lion’s roar:
"Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, and there is no further existence."
"Thus one knows reality as it is: by practicing the realization of *pudgala-nairātmya* (the selflessness of persons), one eventually attains the awakening of *parinirvāṇa*.

Because the śrāvaka’s aversion to suffering is so intense and their urgency to realize the goal is great, when they hear the teaching of the Four Noble Truths—knowing suffering, abandoning its origin, aspiring for cessation, and cultivating the path—their body and mind are filled with joy and serenity.

Although the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas) differ in their individual and common characteristics depending on how they are categorized or condensed, they are nonetheless the Truth of Suffering.
Regarding "knowledge of characteristics" (lakṣaṇajñāna), this is the knowledge of the general characteristics of the Four Noble Truths.

Because the faculties of śrāvakas are dull, they delight in cultivating this knowledge, rather than cultivating the characteristics that lead to awakening through the realization of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
"Conditions" refers to the twelve links of dependent origination, which are what the pratyekabuddhas cultivate to achieve awakening, whereas the śrāvakas do not delight in such cultivation.

By means of the *anantara-samādhi*, the śrāvaka perceives the eighth stage of the pratyekabuddha, severing the active afflictions (*kleśa*) of views and thought, yet they have not severed the ignorance of distinct delusions.
What is called "habitual affliction" is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*).

For this reason, one is unable to transcend the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmika-śīti-bhava*), but can only transcend the sea of suffering of the death and rebirth of segmentation (*prākarṣika-śīti-bhava*).

The "lion's roar" refers to speaking with fearlessness; it means that upon reaching the eighth stage, one declares: "Birth has been exhausted, the accumulation of suffering has been severed; the holy life has been established, and there will be no further existence; the path has been cultivated and cessation has been realized."
"All these are true and not false; therefore, it is said that one knows them as they truly are (*yathābhūtam*).

To cultivate the realization of *pudgala-nairātmya* (the selflessness of persons) up to the attainment of the awakening of *nirvāṇa* means to eliminate the grasping at a person through emptiness and thereby realize true emptiness."

“Mahāmati! As for the various distinct and uninterrupted [conceptions], sentient beings—conceiving themselves as a self, a person, a living being, a life-span, a nourisher, or a spirit—form such perceptions and seek parinirvāṇa.”
Furthermore, according to the teachings of certain heterodox teachers, once they have perceived all natures as being produced by a creator, they declare, "This is parinirvāṇa.
Forming such a realization, they lack the vision of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*); for them, there is no liberation.

Mahāmati! These śrāvakayāna practitioners who possess the lineage of the uninterrupted non-Buddhists lack the realization that they have not yet emerged [from saṃsāra] despite their sense of having emerged; therefore, in order to overturn those evil views, they should practice and study.

Regarding "each distinct and uninterrupted": this refers to Śrāvakas who are attached to signs; they claim to be "uninterrupted" no differently than non-Buddhists. They take various differentiated dharmas—such as views regarding self and person—to be *nirvāṇa*, yet they do not realize that these are the very root of birth and death, instead regarding them as awakening and taking them as a realization.

Furthermore, there is another class who reckon that all phenomena exist solely through volitional construction (*abhisamskāra*) and, misapprehending causes as causes, perceive the nature of all things to be *nirvāṇa*.

Like the Śrāvakas who delight in cessation and cultivate the path, yet for whom liberation through the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is truly not their portion—though they call themselves sons of the Buddha, they are in fact outsiders; thus they are called "uninterrupted outsiders" (*ānantaryatīrthika*).
Although they desire to transcend the three realms, they are unable to do so; hence it is said that they have "the perception of transcendence without having transcended.
This also exhorts students to turn away from those evil views and proceed toward the lineage of the Tathāgata.

“Mahāmati! As for those of the pratyekabuddhayāna lineage who are of the immediate type, when they hear it said that there is an immediate realization through individual conditions, their hair stands on end and they weep with flowing tears. They do not cling to any non-proximate conditions; rather, upon hearing it said that there are various bodies, various supernormal powers, and various transformations—whether separated or joined—their minds enter into accordance with this teaching.”

If one knows that a person possesses the uninterrupted lineage of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, one should accordingly teach them the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; this is called the characteristic of the uninterrupted lineage of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.

As for the *pratyekabuddha* (Pratyeka-jue): having received the teachings from a Buddha, they contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) and awaken to the principle of the True Dharma; thus they are called *pratyekabuddhas*.
They are also called *vivekajina* (Duojue) because they appear in worlds where no Buddha exists and attain self-awakening by observing the conditions of existence.

Regarding those who individually take the immediate [condition] as their object: upon hearing the teaching that the twelve links of dependent origination circulate through cause and effect, they realize non-arising; this accords with their aspirations, and a convergence of sorrowful feelings moves them to tears.

Regarding the phrase "not associating with others" and so forth: it means delighting in solitude and tranquility, practicing the conduct of seclusion, and being unable to become attached to any signs whatsoever. At times, for their sake, one may speak of the transformations of bodily supernormal powers—such as manifesting many bodies from one, or combining many bodies into one—and upon hearing such teachings, their minds enter into them.
The Bodhisattva, knowing that one possesses the lineage of a Pratyekabuddha, should preach this Pratyekabuddha vehicle for them.

"Mahāmati! There are four types of the immediate lineage of the Tathāgata vehicle: namely, the immediate lineage of the nature of phenomena; the immediate lineage of the absence of self-nature in phenomena; the immediate lineage of the noble self-realization; and the immediate lineage of the excellence of external lands."

Mahāmati! If, upon hearing each of these four matters explained one by one, as well as the explanation of the inconceivable realm established through the manifestation of one's own mind, body, and wealth, the mind is not startled or terrified, this is called the characteristic of the lineage of uninterrupted succession in the Tathāgata-yāna.
"The lineage of the Tathāgata is uninterrupted" means that its nature is perfectly interfused and unimpeded.
As for the "four kinds," the first is the dharma of self-nature, which is the intrinsically pure mind of the Tathāgatagarbha.
2. The dharma of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), which means that this nature is free from attachment to intrinsic nature.
3. The attainment of the noble self-awakening, which is the ultimate awakening-wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Fourth, the excellence of external lands refers to the various excellences of the Tathāgata’s compassionate vows in adorning the lands and gathering in sentient beings.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"Regarding the three kinds of realized dharmas, the dharma of intrinsic nature and the dharma apart from intrinsic nature are combined as one; these three kinds are precisely the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Response-body."
Regarding the teaching on the manifestation of one’s own mind as body, wealth, and so forth, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"If, upon hearing that the inconceivable realm of the ālayavijñāna is established as the manifestations of body, wealth, and so forth arising from one’s own mind, one is not startled, terrified, or afraid, it should be known that this person possesses the nature of the Tathāgata-yāna."
“Mahāmati, those of indeterminate lineage are so called because when the three [lineages] are taught, they enter according to what is taught and are established accordingly. Mahāmati!”

This is the first stage of cultivation, namely the establishment of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), which is established for the purpose of transcending into the stage of non-existence (*akiṃcanya*).

As for that "self-realized treasury" (*svasaṃvedanālaya*), when one's own afflictive habit-energies (*kleśavāsanā*) are purified and one perceives the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), one attains the blissful abiding of samādhi as a śrāvaka and shall eventually attain the most supreme body of a Tathāgata.

Regarding those of indeterminate lineage: when they hear the teachings on the three vehicles of the śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and tathāgata, they give rise to faith and understanding accordingly and practice in accordance with them; because they may enter from the small [vehicle] into the great, and their nature is capable of being shifted, they are said to be "indeterminate."

Regarding those who first cultivate the stages: these are the individuals on the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*). For their sake, it is taught that they are of indeterminate lineage; this causes them to transcend and enter the Stage of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-bhūmi*), which is the seventh stage, the Stage of Having Accomplished What Was to Be Done (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*).
"To establish this" means to speak thus. Regarding "that self-realized storehouse" (*svasaṃvedanagarbha*) and so forth, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:

"Those śrāvakas who abide in the bliss of samādhi, if they can realize and know their own foundational consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), perceive the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), and purify the habitual tendencies of afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*), will ultimately attain the body of a Tathāgata."
"The consciousness which serves as its own support is the self-awakening treasury, the eighth consciousness.
The habit-energies of afflictions are ignorance.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The fruit of *srotāpanna*, the *sakṛdāgāmin* and the *anāgāmin*, and the attainment of *arhatship*—these are states where the mind is deluded. Regarding the *srotāpanna*:

this refers to the *srotāpanna*, which is translated here as "Stream-enterer. One is able to sever the delusions of view (*darśana-heya*) within the three realms and enters the stream of the noble ones (*ārya*); this is the first fruit.

Regarding "one who comes and goes" (āgāmin): in Sanskrit this is called *sakṛdāgāmin*. One who has been able to sever the first six grades of the afflictions of desire (*kāmāvacara-kleśa*) but has not yet severed the final three grades, and who will come and go once more among the realms of humans and devas—this is the second fruit.
The Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), in Sanskrit, is one who has exhausted all afflictions of the desire realm and will no longer return to be born there;
this is the third fruit. The Arhat is the fourth fruit.

Although these individuals who have attained the four fruits of the path have severed the afflictions of views and thought and realized the minor fruits, they have not yet been able to sever the two delusions of the "dust-sand" afflictions and ignorance; this constitutes their state of confusion and delusion.
“The three vehicles and the one vehicle—these are not vehicles as I have taught them.
It is for the sake of the foolish who possess little wisdom; the sages remain far removed in tranquility.
The three vehicles refer to the three natures: those of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the indeterminate.
The One Vehicle is the lineage of the Tathāgata;
the non-vehicle refers to the various distinct lineages.

The intention of the Tathāgata is to speak only of the One Vehicle; however, because the capacities of sentient beings are not uniform, he speaks of the three vehicles as "non-vehicles" to lead provisional means back to the ultimate reality.
The various noble ones dwell in seclusion and tranquility; they joyfully enter into nirvana—these are the noble ones of the four fruits.
"The Dharma-gate of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) Is far removed from the two teachings;
Abiding in non-existence, Why establish the three vehicles?"
The gateway of the primary meaning (*paramārtha*) is the principle of quiescence; how could there be any distinction between the provisional and the real?
The Tathāgata abides in this principle of quiescence, wherein not even a single dharma is established, let alone the three vehicles.
“The various dhyānas, the immeasurables, etc., the formless attainments,
and the complete cessation of sensation and perception— therein, even the measure of mind does not exist.
Regarding “the various dhyānas,” these are the four dhyānas.
The "immeasurables" (apramāṇa) refer to the four immeasurable minds.
The "formless" (ārūpya) refers to the four formless absorptions (ārūpyasamāpatti).
"Samādhi" refers to meditative equipoise (samāhita), which is to say, samāpatti.
"The cessation of sensation and perception" refers to the *nirodhasamāpatti* (attainment of cessation) of the Hīnayāna;
